title: Birding in South Sikkim: Kitam, Maenam, Tendong
meta_description: Birding in South Sikkim from 370 m to 3,263 m: Kitam's peafowl and junglefowl, Maenam's tragopans, Tendong's laughingthrushes, best months, guides and ethics.
summary: South Sikkim packs three bird habitats into an hour's drive: Kitam Bird Sanctuary's warm sal and pine forest at 370–980 m, the oak and rhododendron of Tendong at up to 2,600 m, and Maenam Wildlife Sanctuary rising to 3,263 m above Ravangla. Come November to May, start at dawn and hire a local guide.

sections.heading: Why the south works for birders
paras: Birds in the eastern Himalaya sort themselves by altitude, and South Sikkim has an unusually steep spread of it in a small area. From the Rangeet and Teesta valleys around Melli and Jorethang, at roughly 300 to 500 m, the land climbs to the 3,263 m summit of Maenam within about 30 km as the crow flies. That means a birder based at Namchi or Ravangla can work subtropical forest at sunrise and temperate oak and rhododendron by mid-morning, and see two quite different sets of species in a day.

The two big protected areas carry real weight. Maenam Wildlife Sanctuary and the adjoining Tendong Reserve Forest are listed together as an Important Bird Area by BirdLife International, and Kitam Bird Sanctuary, declared on 3 February 2005, protects one of the few patches of low-altitude forest in the state. Sikkim as a whole records well over 500 bird species, and its state bird is the blood pheasant, which lives far higher, in the north and west. The south is where you come for the lower and middle bands.

sections.heading: Kitam: the low forest
paras: Kitam Bird Sanctuary covers only about 6 sq km on the slopes above the Rangeet near Manpur and Melli, about 19 km from Namchi. It is warm, dry forest of sal and pine, more like the Himalayan foothills than the Sikkim most people picture, and it is the place in the state best known for wild Indian peafowl. Listen for their loud calls at first light. The Wikipedia article on the sanctuary also lists red junglefowl, kalij pheasant, oriental white-eye, scarlet minivet, common green magpie and Himalayan flameback among its birds, and barking deer, wild boar and Assamese macaque among its mammals.

Kitam is at its best between November and April, early in the morning, when the air is cool and the birds are active. By 10 am it is hot and quiet. It is also a fine place for butterflies, especially after the monsoon in October. Facilities are basic: forest tracks, a few watch points and village homestays in the area. A forest department entry fee and rules on guides may apply; check current status before you travel.

sections.heading: Tendong: oak and rhododendron
paras: The forest path from Damthang to the 2,600 m summit of Tendong is one of the most pleasant birding walks in Sikkim, because it climbs steadily through unbroken broadleaf forest and you can stop wherever a flock is feeding. Mixed flocks are the main event here: laughingthrushes working the leaf litter, sibias and minlas in the mid-storey, yuhinas and warblers in the canopy, with woodpeckers and barbets calling around them. In March and April the tree rhododendrons flower and nectar-feeding birds gather in them.

Walk up slowly. Birders often take five or six hours for the round trip that walkers do in four. Start at first light, carry water, as there is none on the path, and wear leech socks from June to September. The summit clearing and watchtower give a good view over the canopy for raptors on sunny late mornings.

sections.heading: Maenam: the high forest above Ravangla
paras: Maenam Wildlife Sanctuary, established in 1987, covers about 35 sq km of the ridge that rises behind Ravangla to 3,263 m. Its name is usually explained as a treasure house of medicines, for the medicinal plants of its forests. The main draw for birders is the satyr tragopan, a crimson, blue-faced pheasant of dense undergrowth that is far easier to hear than to see; its wailing calls carry through the forest in the breeding season of April and May. Kalij pheasant, red-faced liocichla, vivid niltava and grey-chinned minivet are among the birds regularly reported by visiting birders, and the sanctuary is also home to red panda and Himalayan black bear, though sightings are rare.

The trail from Ravangla to the Maenam summit is long and steep: about 12 km one way and 5 to 6 hours up, a full day out and back. Most birders do not go to the top, but work the lower and middle sections for half a day. The Bhaleydunga cliff further along the ridge is a longer, guided outing. Take a local guide; the trails branch and cloud comes in quickly.

sections.heading: Birding without a trail: roads and villages
paras: Some of the easiest birding in the south needs no sanctuary at all. The quiet roads around Ravangla, Kewzing and Yangang pass through a patchwork of farms, cardamom gullies under alder trees, bamboo and secondary forest, and at first light the roadside wires and bushes are busy. Verditer flycatchers, grey treepies, bulbuls, blue whistling thrushes, sunbirds and drongos are common, and winter brings altitudinal migrants such as redstarts and thrushes down from higher up.

This is also the best kind of birding for families and older travellers, because you can walk a level stretch of road for an hour with the car following. Homestay hosts in Kewzing and Yangang often know which trees are fruiting and where the barbets gather. The Temi Tea Garden, with its open rows and edge forest, is good for raptors and for small birds in the cherry trees in November.

sections.heading: Guides, gear and ethics
paras: A local bird guide is worth far more than the fee. Several Ravangla and Kitam area guides know the calls, the feeding trees and the gullies where pheasants cross; ask your hotel or homestay a day ahead. For your own kit, bring binoculars (8x42 suits forest birding), a field guide such as Grimmett, Inskipp and Inskipp's Birds of the Indian Subcontinent, a rain jacket and shoes with grip. The eBird app and its hotspot lists for Kitam and Maenam show recent sightings.

Please bird gently. Avoid playback calls in the April–June breeding season, never approach or photograph active nests, stay on paths, keep voices low and carry every bit of litter out. Forest department rules apply inside both sanctuaries, and entry fees or guide requirements change; check current status before you travel.

sections.heading: A four-day birding plan
paras: Base yourself at Namchi for Kitam and at Ravangla for Tendong and Maenam. This is the outline we use for birding guests; it can be stretched to five or six days with a homestay night at Kewzing or Yangang for village-edge birding and a slower morning on each trail.
list: Day 1: arrive Namchi from Siliguri (≈ 100 km · 3.5–4 h); evening on the Samdruptse ridge
Day 2: dawn at Kitam (≈ 19 km from Namchi), back for lunch, drive to Ravangla (≈ 1 h)
Day 3: Tendong from Damthang, a slow full morning on the trail
Day 4: lower Maenam trail from Ravangla at first light, then onward or back to Siliguri

faqs.q: What is the best time for birding in South Sikkim?
faqs.a: November to May. Winter, November to February, brings clear mornings and altitudinal migrants down to Kitam and the village edges. March to May is breeding season, when birds call and colour up and the satyr tragopan calls on Maenam. The monsoon, June to September, is wet, leechy and hard going.

faqs.q: What birds can I see at Kitam Bird Sanctuary?
faqs.a: Kitam is best known for wild Indian peafowl. Its listed birds also include red junglefowl, kalij pheasant, oriental white-eye, scarlet minivet, common green magpie and Himalayan flameback. The sanctuary sits at about 370–980 m in sal and pine forest, so expect foothill species rather than high Himalayan ones.

On the slopes above the Rangeet near Manpur and Melli in Namchi district, about 19 km from Namchi town. It covers about 6 sq km and was declared on 3 February 2005. Namchi or a homestay near Kitam makes the best base for a dawn visit.

faqs.q: Can you see the satyr tragopan in Maenam?
faqs.a: Sometimes, but it is far easier to hear than see. The satyr tragopan lives in dense undergrowth in Maenam Wildlife Sanctuary above Ravangla, and calls loudly in April and May. A local guide who knows its haunts gives you the best chance. Please do not use playback in the breeding season.

faqs.q: How long is the Maenam trek from Ravangla?
faqs.a: About 12 km one way to the 3,263 m summit, typically 5 to 6 hours up and 3 to 4 down, so a full day. Most birders work the lower and middle forest for half a day instead. Take a guide, carry water and start at first light.

faqs.q: Do I need a permit for Maenam or Kitam?
faqs.a: Indian nationals do not need a protected-area permit like those for North Sikkim, but forest department entry fees and guide rules may apply inside both sanctuaries. Foreign nationals need Sikkim's Restricted Area Permit to enter the state. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Is Tendong Hill good for birding?
faqs.a: Yes, very. The 6 km forest path from Damthang to the 2,600 m summit runs through oak and rhododendron where mixed flocks of laughingthrushes, sibias, minlas, yuhinas and warblers feed. Tendong and Maenam together form a BirdLife Important Bird Area. Go early and walk slowly.

faqs.q: Where should birders stay in South Sikkim?
faqs.a: Namchi for Kitam, and Ravangla for Tendong and Maenam. Homestays at Kewzing or Yangang are good for village-edge birding and early starts, and hosts can often put you in touch with local bird guides. A four-to-five-night trip covers all three main sites.

The blood pheasant, a high-altitude pheasant of conifer and rhododendron forest. It lives mostly well above 3,000 m in North and West Sikkim and is not a bird you should expect in the lower South Sikkim forests. The satyr tragopan is the south's signature pheasant.
